**`0063`** -- `check all` reports `all check options passed` while options that never activated appear nowhere. **Reproduced in devbin's own tree: 5 of 8 catalogued options absent, rc 0.** The fix shape is amended into the issue: a PARTITION control (`ran + skipped + inactive == candidates`, refuse when the parts do not sum), not a listing. **The denominator is NOT `lib/builtins` -- it is the deduplicated union `command_options` builds, and `builtin_options` returns empty under a project handler**, so a control reading the catalogue flat would go red in the ordinary case. The inactive set already exists as `seen` minus what printed, four lines apart, and is discarded.

Verified absent twice, once by cc and once here against both nearest neighbours: one is a machine reader truncating a provenance field, the other is a stamp and a live claim being indistinguishable in prose. This one is the mark surviving the file and not the retelling.

**The `fold-compresses-without-testing` residue -- ADDED AS A CLAUSE, not an entry.** _The survivor inherits the fold's authority; a fold reads like a review and is not one._ The mechanism above it is the same one, so a second entry would be the Highlander breach the catalogue exists to avoid. The entry says so in itself.

**cc's `||`-fallback form -- NOT PROMOTED, and this one is deliberate.** cc's own framing is the reason: they suspect it is the same class as `0063` from the other direction -- a summary counting only the options that spoke, and a fallback that cannot tell _I looked and found nothing_ from _I could not look_. **Deciding whether that is one class or two is analysis, not hygiene, and it belongs with sequencing `0063` rather than with a fold.** cc's live instance is written out on their board so it survives without either of us.

Fixture race found at Utilz (their issue 0042, relayed 2026-09-20): a test fixture built with cp -a of a LIVE checkout, .git included, is not an atomic walk. A commit landing mid-copy gives a fixture whose .git carries files its worktree lacks, so git add -A stages deletions and an append-only guard refuses them -- which reads like data loss in the event store and is not. Their fix is ordering: copy .git FIRST and the worktree SECOND, so any tear stages as additions. MEASURED FOR DEVBIN, not assumed: devbin is not exposed. Its three recursive copies (tests/lib/source_fixtures.bash:41-42, tests/lib/test_helper.bash:844) take lib/ and bin/.devbin only, never .git and never the checkout root, and mkdevsrc runs git init plus one commit INSIDE the fixture after the bytes are there, so no pre-existing history can be copied at a different instant from the worktree. Keep this in mind for any future devbin fixture that copies a checkout.

TWO CLOCKS IN ONE DIRECTORY, and it manufactured a false UTC stamp today (dc's gate run, 2026-09-20). devbin's run seals are NAMED in UTC (tmp/test/20260920-1235.bats.out was named at 12:35Z) and ls or stat shows their mtimes in LOCAL time, BST, so the same file reads as 1235 in its name and 13:35 in a listing. dc read a local mtime, appended Z, and reported a window of 13:35Z to 13:52Z whose end had no source at all; both numbers looked consistent because both read 13:xx from two different clocks. Verified here from the seal itself: created 12:35:22Z, last written 13:33:05Z, so the run was 58 minutes, not 17. I reproduced the trap while checking it: stat -t '%H:%M:%SZ' prints a LOCAL time with a Z I supplied, which is a UTC claim made out of a BST number. Read mtimes with TZ=UTC stat, or compare against date -u in the same breath; never append Z to a listing. Sits beside the rule that timestamps come from date -u: this is the same defect arriving through a file listing instead of memory. AND THE LOCAL ZONE IS NOT FIXED AT BST: on 2026-10-08 date read +04 against date -u, so a listing was four hours off UTC, not one (cc's read). The rule does not change: read the zone off the clock every time.

A MECHANISM WHOSE DISABLED STATE IS INDISTINGUISHABLE FROM ITS ENABLED STATE BY INSPECTION -- three instances found on 2026-09-22, in three different tools, none of which reported being off. Silently, since the comment was written, in the one project that arms shellcheck as a critic -- and the sentence written to stress that shellcheck is armed is what disarmed it. Measured: actionlint at HEAD extracted into a clean tree showed the codes predated any edit, and nothing after the reword, so the re-enabled checks came back clean. (b) Laksa ci_cd.yml had a well-formed concurrency block whose cancel-in-progress was ${{ github.event_name == pull_request }} -- cancelling PRs and never pushes, the inverse of hv ruling, and a fleet audit grepping concurrency: counted it compliant. (c) Cdtempl gitignored its devbin manifest for a reason that expired when devbin 0069 made the source path home-relative; the ignore then EXEMPTED the one file anyone suspected from AT-00.6, which greps every TRACKED file for a home path. THE GENERAL FORM: when a guard is configured through a surface that also accepts prose, or through an expression rather than a literal, or by excluding a file from a check, ask what its OFF state looks like -- if it looks identical to ON, only driving it can tell you which it is. A CONSISTENCY CHECK ACROSS COPIES CANNOT SEE AN ERROR COMMON TO EVERY COPY (lamplight/vc, 2026-09-22, and it is the same defect as my 4bdf371 arriving from the other side). Repairing a matcher held in FOUR byte-identical copies, their script ate an escape and wrote a literal backspace byte where a regex backslash-b belonged -- in all four. A backspace matches nothing, so the exclusion silently never fires. Four identical hashes AGREED, and agreed precisely because all four were wrong the same way; the hash check could not have reported it. They found it by reading the BYTES, and read them because four identical hashes felt like weak evidence, which is the judgement worth copying. THE PAIR: my 4bdf371 swept fourteen of cc event files into a commit labelled mine because I staged a DIRECTORY PREFIX, and the repair was to stage by explicit pathspec or subject.id. One is a check too coarse to separate two authors; this is a check too coarse to separate four copies from one common defect. BOTH ARE THE SAME QUESTION: what would this instrument report if the thing I am worried about were true? A hash comparison answers 'are these the same', never 'are these right', and where a repair touched every copy those are different questions. Also from their fix: excluding any path token containing lib/ on the premise that the corpus is never under one was FALSE (content/holmes/lib and content/cosy/lib hold sixteen .lua files), so the fix went blind to the exact coupling the fence exists to catch -- strictly worse than the loud false positive it replaced. critic-elixir caught it.

A CAUTION WRITTEN FROM A SINGLE LIVED INSTANCE INHERITS THAT INSTANCE'S DIRECTION (lamplight/vc, 780946818, 2026-09-22). Lamplight's SdlDrift fence already warned that regenerating the contract is not the whole fix -- fixed on 2026-08-20 after a schema change ADDED filter fields and broke an exhaustive struct literal in ops/frontdesk.rs. Today the same three fields LEFT, frontdesk.rs still named them, and regenerating alone moved the red from Elixir to Rust. A reader following the warning faithfully would have checked whether anything had been added, found nothing, concluded it did not apply, and committed a broken CLI build. The warning was present, accurate, and pointed at the WRONG HALF OF ITS OWN MECHANISM: the mechanism was always any change to the field set, the incident that taught it was an addition, and the text recorded the addition. Different from a missing warning and worse, because it reads as covering the case it excludes. THE CHECK: when writing a caution from an incident, name the MECHANISM and ask what its symmetric case looks like -- a departure as well as an arrival, a shrink as well as a growth -- and say whether the guard catches both. The fence now says any change in both directions and cites both instances, and the exhaustive struct literal is the property worth naming because neither an arrival nor a departure can be silently absent from it. SECOND CLAUSE, same fix: a remedy-text sweep must distinguish INSTRUCTION from DESCRIPTION from QUOTATION, and only the first ages. Eleven citations of a mix task looked like one defect; eight were correct (devbin's contract verb covers generate and check, NOT operations, and there is no playtest verb at all), and of the remaining five only three were remedy text -- one described what the task emits, one quoted the fence's own earlier wording as the record of this defect. A sweep keying on the string rather than the FUNCTION would have replaced eight working instructions with names that resolve to nothing and eaten its own fossil record.

A CONFIRMATION FROM A MACHINE THAT COULD NOT HAVE SHOWN THE SYMPTOM IS CORROBORATION, NOT A SECOND DATA POINT (2026-09-22, gyges session, my judgement call on their report). Gyges reported blob present, ClaudeCodeTriggersInstalled 1, triggers 0, pidinfo idle at 0.1%, load 2.71, and offered it as independent confirmation that the iTerm Workgroups blob is inert without the triggers. The mechanism is per-SESSION: gitStatus walks a tree once per open session, so pidinfo load scales with session count and tree size. The primary machine had ~25 sessions on monorepos. Not vacuous: a BUSY pidinfo there would have contradicted the correction, so the test carries real information; its POWER just depends on a number nobody established. THE STRONG EVIDENCE REMAINS THE PRIMARY MACHINE OWN BEFORE/AFTER: same box, same sessions, one variable, pidinfo 1748 -> 0. THE CHECK, and it is watchout 19 asked of a confirmation rather than a ratio: before recording a second estate or machine as confirming, ask what reading there would have REFUTED it, and whether that reading was even available given the population. Where the population is smaller than the one the symptom needed, record it as corroboration at its honest weight.

A RIGHT NUMBER UNDER THE WRONG NOUN READS AS AUTHORITY AND PROPAGATES; A WRONG NUMBER INVITES CHECKING (gtools/vc, 2026-09-22, naming their own defect better than I did). They cited '6 of 32' as the whiteboard filter's hit rate. They had COPIED MY FIGURE CORRECTLY and attached it to the wrong subject: 6 of 32 is the rate of the PAIR (whiteboard + canon), and the whiteboard line's own rate is ZERO of 32 -- nil, not small, because intent wb writes a canon event beside every board view it renders, so a board-only push is never board-only on disk and GitHub skips only when EVERY changed path matches. THE CLASS IS DISTINCT FROM MY OWN THREE DENOMINATOR ERRORS (watchout 19) AND IS MORE DANGEROUS. THEIR RULE, which I am adopting: a figure that is someone else's travels with its SUBJECT and its DENOMINATOR, both, or it stops meaning anything. Their board already said 'measure a relayed sha, figure or premise at the moment of use' and that was not enough, because the figure was accurate at the moment of use -- the noun was the part that had drifted. PAIRS WITH watchout 20: a premise transfers no better than a rate, and a rate transfers no better than its subject.

ST0007 design review (4b246b2), vc. The shape is right: a builtin with one sequence, postconditions read from the repository and not from a state file, the project declaring facts rather than steps, and one writer per release object. Verified against source: `doctor` exits 1 on a failed `devbin_version` check, so D43's gate claim holds; `publish` is `opt-in` in `lib/builtins`. Seven findings, most serious first. Nothing needs rebuilding from scratch.

**1. D38 runs the gates BEFORE the stamp and the commit, so the tag names a commit no gate examined.** Step 3 gates the pre-stamp tree; step 4 then changes VERSION, sidecars, derived files and the notes views; step 8 tags that. In devbin's own release, `release.bats` holds the committed views to the notes -- so the gate that ran never saw the views that shipped. Proposal: resolve, pre-flight, stamp, commit, THEN gates on the release commit, then CI, confirm, tag. It is still all local and reversible, so principle 3 holds.

**2. Step 3's resume skip contradicts principle 4.** "Skipped on a resume whose release commit exists and whose tree is clean (the gates ran for that commit)" infers that gates passed from the commit existing. With no state file (principle 2), nothing records that they passed: a run that committed and was killed in the gates reads identically. Gates re-run on every resume, or show `already` only when something outside the run proves it, such as a green CI query for that SHA.

**3. D40(a) pushes to `main` before step 7 Confirm.** With `ci:` declared, the first irreversible act happens before the one human confirmation, which principle 3 and step 7 both exist to prevent. Confirm has to come before the first push, whatever hv rules on D40.

**4. `ci.query` answers two different questions.** D37 defines it as "the CI state of a SHA" and step 6 uses it that way. D42 step 10 reuses it to wait for a release OBJECT made by a tag-triggered workflow, which is a different run on a different ref. Two keys, eg `ci.query` for the commit gate and `object_query` (or a `gh release view` built into `object: ci`) for step 10. Otherwise a project with a commit query and a separate release workflow gets `done` from the wrong run.

**5. Pre-flight's clean-tree rule and `bump: given` disagree about the human steps.** D43 leaves writing the note, bumping VERSION and bumping the constraint to the human. If those are uncommitted when `cut` runs -- which is how they were today -- step 2 refuses, because the core did not write them. If they must be committed first, the release is two commits, and D43's walk should say so. Pick one and state it in D38.

**6. D35 `language: any` makes `release` appear in all 16 estates, most of which never release.** The catalogue already has the opt-in activation axis for this (`publish` uses it). Proposal: `opt-in`, active when `commands.release.enabled` is true or a `release:` block is declared. That also cuts the vendoring blast radius: the pre-notice reservation applies to a new builtin, and the design should name it.

**7. D41 against AC 6.** D41 reuses an existing tag at the release commit "whether or not its message matches"; AC 6 says the tag message IS the notes body byte for byte. Scope AC 6 to tags the core makes, and add that a reused tag with a different message is reported.

**One sequencing point for hv, not a defect:** the WP table puts devbin's adoption (WP-07) before Utilz's (WP-08), while hv ruled Utilz the first user. The argument for devbin first is good; it is hv's to confirm, so add it to the questions for hv.

**Proposed AC-3.2:** *Asking a notes verb about a commit materialises that commit's whole tree at a root outside the project and removes it on every exit path including a refusal, so a status run cannot alter the dirt it reports; the limits `git archive` imposes are declared, and the one that can make a correct release read as unstamped -- an export-ignored path -- is refused naming the attribute rather than read as an absent note.*

**Why "outside the project" is in the AC rather than in a comment.** Every notes verb takes the root it reads, so asking about a commit means materialising that commit's whole tree and naming it as the root. If that lands under the project root it is untracked non-ignored dirt -- which is exactly what step 4's cleanliness clause and D38's tree rule read. A status run would then change the fact it reports. It is a one-line defect with no symptom until a release is refused for dirt status itself created.

**The three limits, measured on git 2.55.0 this morning rather than assumed.**
- **LFS**: `git archive` smudges pointers, downloads a missing object and writes `.git/lfs/objects`. So "writes nothing" is stated as the tree, the refs, the remotes and the release object, and the read-only test does NOT assert `.git` is byte-identical -- on an LFS project that assertion is false.
- **Submodules are not archived**: a commit carrying a submodule at `vendor` materialises `vendor` as an EMPTY DIRECTORY. Present, so a path test succeeds; empty, so anything read through it is absent. The worse of the two shapes, because it fails a check rather than the materialisation.
- **`export-ignore`**: driven with a commit holding `.gitattributes`, `drop/b.txt` and `keep/a.txt` and `drop/ export-ignore`, the materialised tree is `.gitattributes` and `keep/a.txt` alone. **This is the one that can make a correct release look unstamped**, silently, so it is the one the AC makes a refusal rather than a declaration.

1. **The `ci.query` contract, which the design leaves open:** it runs as `<query words> <sha>`, the SHA appended the way `notes.run` receives its verb and version. Its first stdout line is `<verdict>[TAB<detail>]`, the verdict one of green, failed, pending, none or unknown, and the detail naming the run (id or url) or the reason. A line that doesn't parse, a non-zero exit, or no output reads as `unknown`, carrying what it said. This is Utilz's install_ci_state shape (`<state>TAB<detail>`), except that Utilz prints gh's own conclusion word (`success`), so its adoption (WP-08) needs a two-line adapter. I'm not bending the core to gh's vocabulary.
2. **Every call that can hang is bounded.** A new `release_run_bounded <seconds> <out> <err> cmd...` in lib/release.steps, the watchdog shape Utilz arrived at (including its 0032 lesson: the watchdog holds no pipe of its caller's). It's used for the query and for step 9's `gh release view` polls. A call cut off at its deadline is `unknown`, naming the deadline. It lives in release.steps, not helpers, because only release needs it today; it moves to helpers when a second caller appears.
3. **Step 9 under `object: ci`:** an object already there is `already`. Otherwise it polls release_read_object (the same reader) every min(15s, time left) until `object_wait`. The result is `done` naming the wait, or `FAILED` naming the missing object and the last answer, UNREADABLE included. It creates nothing, and it never reads a CI verdict (AC-6.1). A dry run is `would`. Step 6 names nothing for it, since the object isn't the core's to make.
4. **Step 10, `after:`:** each command in order, run with run_words from the project root with stdin `</dev/null`, each reported. A failure does NOT stop the run: step 11 still runs, and the cut ends exit 1 saying "the release is published; after: <cmd> failed (exit N)". D38 gives step 10 no postcondition, so a re-run of a finished release runs `after:` again. I'll declare that in the as-built and put it to hv as a question (an announcement run twice), not change it.
5. **Step 11, `ci.query`:** it asks about the RELEASE COMMIT's SHA (the tagged commit), every min(15s, time left) while pending or none, until `ci.wait`. green is row 11 `done` and exit 0. failed or unknown is `FAILED`, naming the detail and the remedy: fix forward and cut the next patch; the tag and the release stand, untouched. That's exit 1. A wait that runs out on pending or none is also `FAILED`, exit 1, "no verdict within <wait>; last: <answer>". **A 0 from a cut that could not confirm green would be a false green**, which is why a timeout is not 0. Dry run: `would`.
6. **The not_yet exits for `object: ci`, `after:` and `ci.query` go.** A cut then runs 1 to 11, and exit 3 leaves release entirely.

LEG CONTRACT (vc's ruling, 2026-10-31; cc and dc build to it; questions to vc, not a second draft).
R = the release commit the stamp step makes; every verdict is keyed on R's sha and a platform. The tested sha is R, pushed to candidate/<tag> on the project's GitHub remote, or under publish.url the snapshot S of R's tree; the RELEASE seal records R and S.
A leg yields one word: green, red, pending, none (no record or not started). Legs: local (the declared gates in place at R on this machine; verdict = the seal pair with commit: R and platform: this one, .errors empty and not in flight); candidate (the matrix on candidate/<tag>, read by the built-in ci-state for the tested sha; Test Summary's verdict; WSL blocks nothing); legs.<name> (a remote host runs the project's own declared gates at R in a worktree of a bare repo on that host; the seal pair is copied back under tmp/release/legs/<name>/ and read by the same reader); macos (sign and notarise at R, where declared; its own seal).
Order: resolve, pre-flight, confirm (the one yes, before anything runs; --yes answers it and sets the confirmed variable the after: commands read), stamp, commit, then every leg starts in one step and one loop reads them all; tag and push only when every leg is green; then object, attach, after (the formula under the yes). The yes names the tag, R, every remote, the object, the assets and the tap.
Already: before a leg starts, its verdict for (sha, platform) is read; a recorded green is already and the leg is not started. Gates keep no other memory.
Loop: poll every ci.poll seconds (15 today), deadline ci.wait (default 60m) from the loop's start, one GitHub read per poll; print one line per state change with the clock. End: all green -> tag; any red -> stop red; deadline -> stop timeout. On stop: kill the local background runs, leave remote legs to finish (their seals are records), delete the candidate ref, nothing public; R stays in local history; the fix lands on top and the same version is cut again while no tag exists (Q3).
Interface: the loop (cc, WP02) calls leg_start <leg> and leg_read <leg> (one word plus a detail line) per leg; cc owns the loop and the local and candidate legs; dc owns legs.<name> (WP05) and macos (WP06) behind the same pair, in files of their own; the one-arm hook-ins into the loop land after WP02. Every verdict goes through WP01's seal reader (the commit: line) or ci-state; nothing else reads one.
Clock: the RELEASE seal gains start: and end: lines (UTC) and one line per leg: name, verdict, sha, duration.
Booking is outside the core: the operator or the coordinating node books the box before the cut; the core never calls intent estate.
Mechanism failure (ssh or gh unreachable) reads as none with its reason printed; at the deadline it is a timeout. No silent errors.
